```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(flowCore)
  library(flowWorkspace)
  library(openCyto)
  library(ggcyto)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
})

kOutputDir <- file.path("..", "output", "automated_gating_pbmc")

ReadOutput <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path(kOutputDir, name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop(
      "The analysis output is missing: ", path, "\n",
      "Run scripts/01_automated_gating_pbmc.R first."
    )
  }
  read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)
}

OutputImage <- function(name) {
  file.path(kOutputDir, name)
}
```

## What this report does

This report works through a complete flow cytometry analysis in R. It reads
eight FCS files, applies the compensation matrix that the instrument wrote
into them, transforms the fluorescence channels, and gates every sample with
one openCyto template. It then reports the frequency of each population and
the spread of those frequencies across the eight samples.

The report does not repeat the analysis. It reads the files that
`scripts/01_automated_gating_pbmc.R` wrote, and every number below comes
from one run of that script, so a new render cannot change a result.

### Why the gate hierarchy is a CSV

The gate hierarchy is in `gating/pbmc_gating_template.csv`, not in this
document and not in a workspace file. A gate drawn by hand lives inside a
FlowJo workspace, and to know what a colleague did, you open their workspace
and you look. A template is a text file. A reviewer reads it in a pull
request, a version control system records who changed a cut point, and the
same file gates the next experiment.

Maecker and colleagues sent pre-stained cells to 15 experienced
laboratories. Local gating gave a mean CV of 20.5 percent, and central
gating of the same raw files gave 4 percent [1]. The template is the
mechanism that makes central gating practical, because the analysis moves
instead of the analyst.

## The dataset

```{r}
#| label: sample-sheet

sample_sheet <- ReadOutput("sample_sheet.csv")
kable(
  sample_sheet[, c("file_name", "donor", "condition", "well", "stimulated")],
  caption = "The eight files, with the design parsed from the file names."
)
```

The design has two donors and four stimulation conditions, where `NS` means
not stimulated and `PI` means stimulated with PMA and ionomycin. The files
were acquired on an LSRII on 18 January 2013, and they come from the FlowJo
Basic Tutorial.

```{r}
#| label: event-counts

event_counts <- ReadOutput("event_counts.csv")
kable(event_counts, caption = "Events acquired per sample.")
```

### The panel

```{r}
#| label: panel

panel <- ReadOutput("panel.csv")
kable(panel, caption = "Detectors and markers. A row with no marker is scatter or time.")
```

Two properties of this panel decide what the analysis can do. There is a
viability dye, so the analysis excludes dead cells instead of keeping them,
and there is `FSC-H` beside `FSC-A`, so the analysis excludes doublets. A
panel with only `FSC-A` cannot gate singlets at all, and a doublet then
counts as a cell in every population below it.

## Compensation

Spillover is the light from one fluorochrome that a second detector also
reads. The relationship is linear, so the correction multiplies the measured
values by the inverse of the spillover matrix. These files carry the matrix
in the FCS `$SPILLOVER` keyword, which the acquisition software wrote from
single stained controls, and the analysis reads that matrix and applies it.

```{r}
#| label: spillover-top

spillover_top <- ReadOutput("spillover_top10.csv")
spillover_top$percent <- round(100 * spillover_top$spill, 2)
kable(
  spillover_top[, c("from", "to", "percent")],
  caption = "The ten largest spillover values, as a percentage.",
  col.names = c("From detector", "Into detector", "Spillover, percent")
)
```

The largest value names the pair of detectors that compensation actually
moves.

```{r}
#| label: spillover-matrix

spillover <- as.matrix(read.csv(
  file.path(kOutputDir, "spillover_matrix.csv"),
  row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE
))
kable(
  round(spillover, 3),
  caption = "The full spillover matrix. The diagonal is 1 by construction."
)
```

### Doing this without a stored matrix

When the file carries no matrix, compute one from single stained controls
with `flowStats::spillover_ng()`. In Python the equivalent is a
`flowkit.Matrix` built from the controls. The common mistake is to
compensate with a matrix from a different acquisition day, and that mistake
produces a population that does not exist.

## Transformation

Fluorescence data spans several orders of magnitude, and after compensation
it holds negative values, which a log transform cannot represent. The
logicle transform is linear near zero and logarithmic above it, so the
negative population stays visible and the positive population stays
separated.

```{r}
#| label: transform-channels

channels <- readLines(file.path(kOutputDir, "transformed_channels.txt"))
cat("Transformed channels:\n")
cat(paste0("  ", channels, collapse = "\n"))
```

One transform is estimated on the first sample and applied to all eight,
because a per sample estimate would move a gate between samples for a reason
that has nothing to do with the biology.

## The gating template

```{r}
#| label: template

template <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "pbmc_gating_template.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(
  template[, c("alias", "pop", "parent", "dims", "gating_method")],
  caption = "The gating template. Each row is one population."
)
```

The `nonDebris` row says to take
`root` and, on `FSC-A` and `SSC-A`, fit a `flowClust` gate and keep the
positive population.

The template fixes the method and the channels, but it does not fix the cut
point. openCyto fits every gate on every sample separately, so a sample
whose distribution sits slightly differently still gets its own boundary.
That is the difference between a template and a copied gate.

```{r}
#| label: gating-tree
#| fig-cap: "The gate hierarchy that the template produced."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("gating_tree.png"))
```

## The gates

Each figure shows one gate on the first sample, and the fitted boundary is
drawn on the data it was fitted to.

```{r}
#| label: gate-figures
#| results: asis

populations <- readLines(file.path(kOutputDir, "population_paths.txt"))
populations <- setdiff(populations, "root")

for (population in populations) {
  image_name <- paste0(
    "gate_", gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", population), ".png"
  )
  image_path <- OutputImage(image_name)
  if (file.exists(image_path)) {
    cat("\n\n### ", population, "\n\n", sep = "")
    cat("![](", image_path, ")\n\n", sep = "")
  }
}
```

## Results

### Frequency of every population

```{r}
#| label: population-stats

population_stats <- ReadOutput("population_stats.csv")
kable(
  population_stats[, c("sample", "population", "count", "percent_of_parent")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Event count and percentage of the parent population, per sample."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: frequency-plot
#| fig-cap: "Population frequency by condition. One template gated all eight samples."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("population_frequencies.png"))
```

### Spread across the eight samples

This is the number that the example exists to produce.

```{r}
#| label: spread

spread <- ReadOutput("population_spread.csv")
kable(
  spread,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation of each population frequency across all eight samples."
)
```

The coefficient of variation here holds the biological difference between
two donors, the difference between four stimulation conditions, and the
technical spread of the assay. It holds no analyst variation, because one
template gated every sample. That last point is the purpose of the example.
Add eight analysts who draw their own gates on these same eight files, and
the CV rises with no event changed.

McNeil and colleagues measured this directly. 110 laboratories gated one
shared set of files, they produced 110 different gating approaches, and the
standard deviations were 2.5 to 25 times larger under laboratory specific
gating than under a consensus protocol [2].

```{r}
#| label: spread-by-condition

spread_by_condition <- ReadOutput("population_spread_by_condition.csv")
kable(
  spread_by_condition,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The same statistics, split by stimulation condition. Splitting removes the between condition difference from the spread."
)
```

The pooled CV mixes the stimulation effect into the
spread, and the split CV does not, so it is closer to a measure of the assay
itself.

## Reproducing this

```bash
# Pull the dataset, about 207 MB of the 103 GB archive
./sync.sh pull datasets/flowjo

# Build the container. Every package version is pinned and asserted at build time.
./containers/build.sh

# Run the analysis
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  Rscript scripts/01_automated_gating_pbmc.R

# Render this report
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  quarto render reports/automated_gating_pbmc.qmd
```

```{r}
#| label: session-info

sessionInfo()
```
